Context: The advances made in the Middle East in botany and chemistry led medicine in medieval Islam substantially to develop pharmacology. Muhammad ibn Zakarīya Rāzi (Rhazes) (865-915), for instance, acted to promote the medical uses of chemical compounds. Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (Abulcasis) (936-1013) pioneered the preparation of medicines by sublimation and distillation. His Liber servitoris is of particular interest, as it provides the reader with recipes and explains how to prepare the `simples’ from which were compounded the complex drugs then generally used. Sabur Ibn Sahl (d 869), was, however, the first physician to initiate pharmacopoedia, describing a large variety of drugs and remedies for ailments. Al-Biruni (973-1050) wrote one of the most valuable Islamic works on pharmacology, entitled Kitab al-Saydalah (The Book of Drugs), in which he detailed the properties of drugs and outlined the role of pharmacy and the functions and duties of the pharmacist. Avicenna, too, described no less than 700 preparations, their properties, modes of action, and their indications. He devoted in fact a whole volume to simple drugs in The Canon of Medicine. Of great impact were also the works by al-Maridini of Baghdad and Cairo, and Ibn al-Wafid (1008-1074), both of which were printed in Latin more than fifty times, appearing as De Medicinis universalibus et particularibus by 'Mesue' the younger, and the Medicamentis simplicibus by 'Abenguefit'. Peter of Abano (1250-1316) translated and added a supplement to the work of al-Maridini under the title De Veneris. Al-Muwaffaq’s contributions in the field are also pioneering. Living in the 10th century, he wrote The foundations of the true properties of Remedies, amongst others describing arsenious oxide, and being acquainted with silicic acid. He made clear distinction between sodium carbonate and potassium carbonate, and drew attention to the poisonous nature of copper compounds, especially copper vitriol, and also lead compounds. He also describes the distillation of sea-water for drinking.[verification needed]

Context: Immunology is a science that investigates the structure and function of the immune system; it derives from medicine and early investigations into the causes of immunity to disease. The earliest known reference to immunity occurs during the plague of Athens in 430 BC; Thucydides noted that persons who had recovered from a previous attack of the disease could attend the sick without contracting the illness a second time. In the 18th century, Pierre-Louis Moreau de Maupertuis conducted experiments with scorpion venom and observed that certain dogs and mice were immune to this venom; this and other observations of acquired immunity were later employed by Louis Pasteur in his development of vaccination and his proposed germ theory of disease. Pasteur's theory stood in direct opposition to contemporary theories of disease, such as the miasma theory; it was not until Robert Koch's proofs of 1891, for which he was awarded a Nobel Prize in 1905, that microorganisms were confirmed as the cause of infectious disease. Viruses were established as human pathogens in 1901, with the discovery of the yellow fever virus by Walter Reed.

Context: In 1846, the natural history lectures of Louis Agassiz were acclaimed both in New York and upon the campus of Harvard College; his approach was distinctly idealist, positing Americans' "participation in the Divine Nature" and the possibility of understanding "intellectual existences". Agassiz's perspective on science combined observation with intuition, and it held that a person can grasp the "divine plan" in all phenomena. When explaining life-forms, Agassiz resorted to matters of shape based on a presumed archetype for his evidence; this dual view of knowledge was in concert with the teachings of Common Sense Realism derived from the Scottish philosophers Thomas Reid and Dugald Stewart, whose works formed part of the Harvard curriculum at the time. The popularity of Agassiz's efforts to "soar with Plato" probably derived also from other writings to which Harvard students were exposed, including Platonic treatises by Ralph Cudworth, John Norris, and, in a Romantic vein, Samuel Coleridge. The library records at Harvard reveal that the writings of Plato and his early modern and Romantic followers were almost as regularly read during the 19th century as those of the "official philosophy" of the more empirical and more deistic Scottish school.
Question: in 1846 who's natural history lectures were acclaimed in New York and Harvard?

Context: On May 3, 1901, downtown Jacksonville was ravaged by a fire that originated as a kitchen blaze. Spanish moss at a nearby mattress factory was quickly engulfed in flames, enabling the fire to spread with great rapidity. Within eight hours, it swept through 146 city blocks; it destroyed over 2,000 buildings, left about 10,000 persons homeless, and resulted in the death of 7 residents. The Confederate Monument in Hemming Park was one of the few landmarks to survive the conflagration. Governor Jennings declare martial law and sent the state militia to maintain order. On May 17, municipal authority was restored in Jacksonville. It was reported that the glow from the flames could be seen in Savannah, Georgia, and that smoke plumes were observed in Raleigh, North Carolina. Known as the "Great Fire of 1901", it was one of the worst disasters in Florida history and the largest urban fire in the southeastern United States. Architect Henry John Klutho was a primary figure in the reconstruction of the city. The first multi-story structure built by Klutho was the Dyal-Upchurch Building in 1902. The St. James Building, constructed on the previous site of the St. James Hotel that burned down, was built in 1912 as Klutho's crowning achievement.

Thus, the marginal utility of wealth per person - termed "the additional dollar" - decreases as an individual becomes richer. Context: In the 1890s, the University of Chicago, apprehensive that its considerable resources might prove injurious to smaller institutions by attracting able students, entered into affiliations with several regional colleges and universities, to wit: Des Moines College, Kalamazoo College, Butler University, and Stetson University. In the year 1896, the university formed an affiliation with Shimer College, situated in Mount Carroll, Illinois. According to the terms of this affiliation, the schools were required to maintain courses of study comparable to those of the university, to furnish early notification of any intended faculty appointments or dismissals, to make no faculty appointment without the approval of the university, and to transmit copies of examinations for review. The University of Chicago agreed to confer a degree upon any graduating senior of an affiliated school who achieved a grade of A throughout the four years, as well as upon any other graduate who completed twelve weeks of additional study at the University of Chicago. Any student or faculty member of an affiliated school was entitled to free tuition at the University of Chicago, and students of Chicago were eligible to attend an affiliated school upon identical terms and to receive credit for their labours. Moreover, the University of Chicago agreed to furnish affiliated schools with books, scientific apparatus, and supplies at cost; with special instructors and lecturers at no expense save that of travel; and with a copy of every book and journal issued by the University of Chicago Press without charge. It was stipulated in the agreement that either party might terminate the affiliation upon due notice. Several professors of the University of Chicago disapproved of the programme, inasmuch as it entailed additional labour without compensation on their part, and they held that it degraded the academic standing of the university. The programme, in time, passed into history by the year 1910.

Context: In 1271, Kublai Khan imposed the name Great Yuan (Chinese: 大元; pinyin: Dà Yuán; Wade-Giles: Ta-Yüan), establishing the Yuan dynasty. "Dà Yuán" (大元) is from the sentence "大哉乾元" (dà zai Qián Yuán / "Great is Qián, the Primal") in the Commentaries on the Classic of Changes (I Ching) section regarding Qián (乾). The counterpart in Mongolian language was Dai Ön Ulus, also rendered as Ikh Yuan Üls or Yekhe Yuan Ulus. In Mongolian, Dai Ön (Great Yuan) is often used in conjunction with the "Yeke Mongghul Ulus" (lit. "Great Mongol State"), resulting in Dai Ön Yeke Mongghul Ulus (Mongolian script: ), meaning "Great Yuan Great Mongol State". The Yuan dynasty is also known as the "Mongol dynasty" or "Mongol Dynasty of China", similar to the names "Manchu dynasty" or "Manchu Dynasty of China" for the Qing dynasty. Furthermore, the Yuan is sometimes known as the "Empire of the Great Khan" or "Khanate of the Great Khan", which particularly appeared on some Yuan maps, since Yuan emperors held the nominal title of Great Khan. Nevertheless, both terms can also refer to the khanate within the Mongol Empire directly ruled by Great Khans before the actual establishment of the Yuan dynasty by Kublai Khan in 1271.

Context: Upon the death of Yesün Temür in Shangdu in the year 1328, Tugh Temür was recalled to Khanbaliq by El Temür, the Qipchaq commander. He was installed as Emperor Wenzong in Khanbaliq; meanwhile, Ragibagh, the son of Yesün Temür, succeeded to the throne in Shangdu, supported by Dawlat Shah, the favourite retainer of the late emperor. Having secured the support of princes and officers in Northern China and other regions of the dynasty, Tugh Temür, who was based in Khanbaliq, eventually prevailed in the civil war against Ragibagh, a conflict known as the War of the Two Capitals. Subsequently, Tugh Temür abdicated in favour of his brother Kusala, who had the backing of Chagatai Khan Eljigidey, and declared that Khanbaliq would welcome him. However, Kusala died suddenly after only four days following a banquet with Tugh Temür. It is said that he was poisoned by El Temür, whereupon Tugh Temür resumed the throne. Moreover, Tugh Temür sent delegates to the western Mongol khanates, including the Golden Horde and the Ilkhanate, and was accepted as the suzerain of the Mongol world. Nevertheless, during the latter three years of his reign, he was in large measure a puppet of the powerful official El Temür. El Temür purged the officials who favoured Kusala and elevated warlords to power, whose despotic rule marked the clear decline of the dynasty.

Context: The Yuan dynasty marked the first occasion upon which non-native Chinese people exercised rule over all of China. Within the historiography of Mongolia, it is generally regarded as the continuation of the Mongol Empire. The Mongols are widely known to worship the Eternal Heaven, and, according to traditional Mongolian ideology, the Yuan is considered to be "the beginning of an infinite number of beings, the foundation of peace and happiness, state power, the dream of many peoples, besides it there is nothing great or precious." In the traditional historiography of China, on the other hand, the Yuan dynasty is usually considered the legitimate dynasty falling between the Song dynasty and the Ming dynasty. It should be noted, however, that the Yuan dynasty is traditionally often extended to cover the period of the Mongol Empire prior to Kublai Khan's formal establishment of the Yuan in 1271; this is partly because Kublai had his grandfather Genghis Khan placed on the official record as the dynasty's founder, or Taizu (Chinese: 太祖). Despite the traditional historiography as well as official views, including those of the Ming dynasty which overthrew the Yuan, there also exist Chinese people[who?] who do not consider the Yuan dynasty a legitimate dynasty of China, but rather view it as a period of foreign domination. These latter hold that Han Chinese were treated as second-class citizens[citation needed] and that China stagnated both economically and scientifically.
Question: The Yuan was the first time all of China was ruled by whom?
Answer:

Context: The bureaucratic system devised by Kublai Khan mirrored the diverse cultures present within the empire, encompassing those of the Han Chinese, Khitans, Jurchens, Mongols, and Tibetan Buddhists. Although the official terminology of these institutions might suggest a governmental framework almost entirely derived from native Chinese dynasties, the Yuan bureaucracy was, in fact, a composite of elements from various cultures. The Chinese-style components of the bureaucracy were primarily drawn from the native Tang and Song dynasties, as well as the Khitan Liao and Jurchen Jin dynasties. Chinese advisers, such as Liu Bingzhong and Yao Shu, exerted considerable influence upon Kublai's early court, and the central administration of government was established within the first decade of Kublai's reign. This government adopted the traditional Chinese tripartite division of authority among civil, military, and censorial offices, including the Central Secretariat (Zhongshu Sheng) to manage civil affairs, the Privy Council (Chinese: 樞密院) to manage military affairs, and the Censorate to conduct internal surveillance and inspection. The actual functions of both central and local government institutions, however, exhibited a considerable overlap between civil and military jurisdictions, owing to the Mongol traditional reliance upon military institutions and offices as the core of governance. Nevertheless, such a civilian bureaucracy, with the Central Secretariat as the preeminent institution that was (directly or indirectly) responsible for most other governmental agencies (such as the traditional Chinese-style Six Ministries), was created in China. At various times another central government institution called the Department of State Affairs (Shangshu Sheng), which dealt principally with finance, was established (as during the reign of Külüg Khan or Emperor Wuzong), but was usually abandoned shortly afterwards.

Context: There existed, during the Yuan dynasty, a plurality of religions, including Buddhism, Islam, and Christianity. On the contrary, Kublai Khan, its founder, favoured Buddhism, particularly the Tibetan variants; consequently, Tibetan Buddhism became the de facto state religion. Inasmuch as Kublai Khan esteemed only the Sakya sect of Tibetan Buddhism, other religions were rendered less important. He and his successors maintained a Sakya Imperial Preceptor (Dishi) at court; before the dynasty's end, 14 leaders of the Sakya sect had held this post, thereby enjoying special power. Furthermore, Mongol patronage of Buddhism gave rise to numerous monuments of Buddhist art. Mongolian Buddhist translations, nearly all derived from Tibetan originals, were commenced on a large scale after 1300. Context: The system of government established by Kublai Khan was, in political respects, the outcome of a compromise between Mongolian patrimonial feudalism and the traditional Chinese autocratic-bureaucratic system. Socially, however, the educated Chinese elite were not, in general, accorded the degree of esteem that had been theirs under native Chinese dynasties. Although the traditional Chinese elite were denied their share of power, the Mongols and the Semuren-various allied groups from Central Asia and the western extremity of the empire-remained, for the most part, strangers to mainstream Chinese culture; this dichotomy imparted to the Yuan regime a somewhat pronounced "colonial" colour. The unequal treatment may be attributed to the fear of transferring power to the ethnic Chinese under Mongol rule. Advantages were conferred upon the Mongols and Semuren within the dynasty, and these persisted even after the restoration of the imperial examination in the early 14th century. In general, few North Chinese or Southerners attained the highest posts in government, particularly when compared with the possibility that Persians did so in the Ilkhanate. The Yongle Emperor of the Ming dynasty later remarked upon the discrimination that had existed during the Yuan dynasty. In response to an objection regarding the use of "barbarians" in his government, the Yongle Emperor answered: "... Discrimination was used by the Mongols during the Yuan dynasty, who employed only "Mongols and Tartars" and discarded northern and southern Chinese and this was precisely the cause that brought disaster upon them".
Question: What Mongolian system did Kublai's government compromise with?

Context: Following the Greeks, little progress was made in the study of prime numbers until the advent of the 17th century. In 1640 Pierre de Fermat stated, without proof, what is now called Fermat's little theorem, a result later proved by Leibniz and Euler. Fermat also conjectured that all numbers of the form 22n + 1 are prime, these being termed Fermat numbers, and he verified this property up to n = 4 (or 216 + 1). The very next number of this type, however, is composite; 232 + 1 has the prime factor 641, as Euler later demonstrated, and in fact no further Fermat primes have been discovered. Context: The evolutionary strategy employed by cicadas of the genus Magicicada utilises prime numbers. These insects spend the greater part of their lives as grubs beneath the ground. They pupate only after 7, 13, or 17 years, and thereafter emerge from their burrows; whereupon they take flight, breed, and die within a few weeks at the most. The rationale for this is thought to be that the intervals of prime numbers between emergences render it exceedingly difficult for predators to evolve which might specialise as predators upon Magicicadas. Were Magicicadas to appear at intervals not composed of prime numbers, for instance every 12 years, then predators appearing every 2, 3, 4, 6, or 12 years would infallibly encounter them. Over a 200-year period, the mean populations of predators during hypothetical outbreaks of 14- and 15-year cicadas would be as much as 2 per cent. higher than during outbreaks of 13- and 17-year cicadas. Albeit small, this advantage seems to have sufficed to direct natural selection in favour of a life-cycle based upon prime numbers for these insects.

Context: The notion of prime number possesses such fundamental importance that it has been generalized in various branches of mathematics. The word "prime", generally, denotes a quality of minimality or indecomposability, in an appropriate sense. In field theory, for instance, the prime field constitutes the smallest subfield of a given field F which contains both 0 and 1; this field is either Q or the finite field with p elements, whence its name. Frequently, a further meaning is intended by the term prime, namely that any object can be, essentially uniquely, decomposed into its prime components. In knot theory, a prime knot is defined as a knot which is indecomposable in the sense that it cannot be written as the knot sum of two nontrivial knots; any knot can be uniquely expressed as a connected sum of prime knots. Prime models and prime 3-manifolds constitute other examples of this latter type.

Context: The various forms of the name Rhine in the modern tongues are all derived from the Gaulish name Rēnos; this name was adapted in the geography of the Roman era (1st century BC) as Greek Ῥῆνος (Rhēnos) and Latin Rhenus.[note 3] The spelling with Rh- in English Rhine, as well as in German Rhein and French Rhin, is due to the influence of Greek orthography, whereas the vocalisation -i- results from the Proto-Germanic adoption of the Gaulish name as *Rīnaz; through Old Frankish, it yielded Old English Rín, Old High German Rīn, and Dutch Rijn (formerly also spelled Rhijn). The diphthong in modern German Rhein (adopted also in Romansh Rein and Rain) is a Central German development of the early modern period; the Alemannic name Rī(n) retains the older vocalism,[note 4] as does Ripuarian Rhing, while Palatine has diphthongized to Rhei and Rhoi. Context: The various forms of the name Rhine in the modern tongues are all derived from the Gaulish name Rēnos; this name was adapted in the geography of the Roman era (1st century BC) as Greek Ῥῆνος (Rhēnos) and Latin Rhenus.[note 3] The spelling with Rh- in English Rhine, as well as in German Rhein and French Rhin, is due to the influence of Greek orthography, whereas the vocalisation -i- results from the Proto-Germanic adoption of the Gaulish name as *Rīnaz; through Old Frankish, it yielded Old English Rín, Old High German Rīn, and Dutch Rijn (formerly also spelled Rhijn). The diphthong in modern German Rhein (adopted also in Romansh Rein and Rain) is a Central German development of the early modern period; the Alemannic name Rī(n) retains the older vocalism,[note 4] as does Ripuarian Rhing, while Palatine has diphthongized to Rhei and Rhoi. Spanish, with French, adopts the Germanic vocalism Rin-, while Italian, Occitan, and Portuguese retain the Latin Ren-.

Context: The configuration of the Rhine delta is governed by two principal bifurcations: at Millingen aan de Rijn, the Rhine divides into the Waal and the Pannerdens Kanaal, the latter of which assumes the name Nederrijn at Angeren; near Arnhem, the IJssel departs from the Nederrijn. Thus are formed three principal courses, of which two undergo frequent changes of name. The most considerable and southerly main branch commences as the Waal, and proceeds successively as the Boven Merwede ("Upper Merwede"), the Beneden Merwede ("Lower Merwede"), the Noord River ("North River"), the Nieuwe Maas ("New Meuse"), Het Scheur ("the Rip"), and the Nieuwe Waterweg ("New Waterway"). The middle course begins as the Nederrijn, then changes into the Lek, and subsequently joins the Noord, thereby forming the Nieuwe Maas. The northerly course retains the name IJssel until it flows into Lake IJsselmeer. Three additional flows carry considerable volumes of water: the Nieuwe Merwede ("New Merwede"), which branches off from the southerly branch where it changes from the Boven to the Beneden Merwede; the Oude Maas ("Old Meuse"), which departs from the southerly branch where it changes from the Beneden Merwede into the Noord; and the Dordtse Kil, which branches off from the Oude Maas.

Context: The geological period termed the Ice Ages extended from approximately 2.5 million years ago to 11,600 years ago. Since about 600,000 years ago, six major Ice Ages have transpired, during which the sea level fell 120 metres (390 feet), and a considerable portion of the continental margins was exposed. In the Early Pleistocene, the Rhine pursued a northwesterly course, traversing what is now the North Sea. During the so-called Anglian glaciation, which occurred some 450,000 years before the present and corresponds to marine oxygen isotope stage 12, the northern part of the present North Sea was blocked by ice, and a vast lake came into being, which discharged through the English Channel. This circumstance led to the diversion of the Rhine's course through the English Channel. Thereafter, during glacial periods, the mouth of the river was situated offshore of Brest, in France, and rivers such as the Thames and the Seine were incorporated as tributaries of the Rhine. During interglacial epochs, when the sea level rose to roughly its present level, the Rhine deposited deltas in the region that is now the Netherlands.

Context: From approximately ~3000 yr BP (= years Before Present), the influence of man is observable in the delta. Owing to the progressive clearance of land for agriculture during the Bronze Age in the upland regions of central Germany, the sediment load carried by the Rhine was greatly increased, and the growth of the delta accelerated accordingly. This brought about more frequent flooding and sedimentation, which terminated the formation of peat within the delta. The principal mechanism by which sediment was distributed across the subrecent delta was the shifting of river channels to new positions on the floodplain, a process termed avulsion. Over the past 6000 years, approximately 80 avulsions have occurred. Direct human interference in the delta commenced with the mining of peat for salt and fuel from the Roman era onward. This was succeeded by the embankment of the major distributaries and the damming of the minor ones, which occurred during the 11-13th century AD. Subsequently, canals were excavated, bends were cut short, and groynes were erected to prevent the river's channels from migrating or becoming silted up.

Context: The Rhine was unknown to Herodotus; it first enters the historical period in the 1st century BC, as recorded in Roman-era geography. At that time, it formed the boundary between Gaul and Germania. The Upper Rhine had been part of the areal of the late Hallstatt culture since the 6th century BC; by the 1st century BC, the areal of the La Tène culture covered almost its entire length, thereby forming a contact zone with the Jastorf culture, i.e. the locus of early Celtic-Germanic cultural contact. In Roman geography, the Rhine formed the boundary between Gallia and Germania by definition; e.g. Maurus Servius Honoratus, Commentary on the Aeneid of Vergil (8.727) (Rhenus) fluvius Galliae, qui Germanos a Gallia dividit "(The Rhine is a) river of Gaul, which divides the Germanic people from Gaul."

Context: From the death of Augustus in AD 14 until after AD 70, Rome acknowledged as her Germanic frontier the water-boundary of the Rhine and the upper Danube; beyond these rivers, she held only the fertile plain of Frankfurt, opposite the Roman fortress of Moguntiacum (Mainz), the southernmost slopes of the Black Forest, and a few scattered bridge-heads. The northern section of this frontier, where the Rhine is deep and broad, remained the Roman boundary until the empire fell; the southern part, however, was different, for the upper Rhine and upper Danube are easily crossed. The frontier thus formed is inconveniently long, enclosing an acute-angled wedge of foreign territory between the modern Baden and Württemberg. The Germanic populations of these lands appear to have been scanty in Roman times, and Roman subjects from the modern Alsace-Lorraine had drifted across the river eastwards.

Context: By the 6th century, the Rhine lay within the borders of Francia. In the 9th, it formed part of the boundary between Middle and Western Francia; but in the 10th century, it was fully within the Holy Roman Empire, flowing through Swabia, Franconia, and Lower Lorraine. The mouths of the Rhine, in the county of Holland, fell to the Burgundian Netherlands in the 15th century; Holland remained a subject of contention throughout the European wars of religion and the eventual collapse of the Holy Roman Empire, whereupon the entire course of the Rhine fell to the First French Empire and its dependent states. The Alsace on the left bank of the Upper Rhine was sold to Burgundy by Archduke Sigismund of Austria in 1469 and eventually fell to France during the Thirty Years' War. The numerous historic castles in Rhineland-Palatinate bear witness to the importance of the river as a commercial route.

Context: Since the Peace of Westphalia, the Upper Rhine formed a contentious border between France and Germany. Establishing "natural borders" on the Rhine was a long-term goal of French foreign policy, since the Middle Ages, though the language border was - and is - far more to the west. French leaders, such as Louis XIV and Napoleon Bonaparte, tried with varying degrees of success to annex lands west of the Rhine. The Confederation of the Rhine was established by Napoleon, as a French client state, in 1806 and lasted until 1814, during which time it served as a significant source of resources and military manpower for the First French Empire. In 1840, the Rhine crisis, prompted by French prime minister Adolphe Thiers's desire to reinstate the Rhine as a natural border, led to a diplomatic crisis and a wave of nationalism in Germany.

Context: Imperialism and colonialism alike assert political and economic preponderance over a land and its indigenous inhabitants; yet scholars often find it difficult to distinguish the one from the other. Although both systems involve the suppression of another people, colonialism may be defined as the process by which a nation acquires physical control of another territory, whereas imperialism denotes political and financial dominance, whether exercised formally or informally. Colonialism serves as the architect of domination in given areas, while imperialism furnishes the ideological impetus for conquest, the two cooperating in practice. In essence, colonialism commences when an imperial power begins the conquest of an area and gradually establishes rule over lands formerly held by another nation. The core meaning of colonialism lies in the exploitation of the valuable resources and supplies of the conquered nation, the conquering power then reaping the benefits of the spoils. Imperialism, on the other hand, aims to create an empire by subduing other states' territories, thereby enhancing its own supremacy. Colonialism further acts as the builder and preserver of colonial possessions in a region through the settlement of a population from a foreign land. It can entirely transform the existing social order, physical infrastructure, and economy of an area; indeed, it is not uncommon for the characteristics of the conquerors to be inherited by the conquered indigenous populations.

Context: In English-language academic discourse, theories of imperialism are frequently founded upon the British experience. The term "Imperialism" was first introduced into the English language in its current sense in the late 1870s by opponents of the allegedly aggressive and ostentatious imperial policies of British prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli. It was soon thereafter appropriated by supporters of "imperialism", such as Joseph Chamberlain. For some, imperialism signified a policy of idealism and philanthropy; for others, it was characterised by political self-interest, and a growing number associated it with the greed of capital. The Liberal John A. Hobson and the Marxist Vladimir Lenin imparted a more theoretical macroeconomic connotation to the term. Lenin, in particular, exerted a substantial influence upon later Marxist conceptions of imperialism through his work Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism. In his writings, Lenin portrayed Imperialism as a natural outgrowth of capitalism, arising from the need for capitalist economies to constantly expand investment, material resources, and manpower in such a manner as to necessitate colonial expansion. This conception of imperialism as a structural feature of capitalism is echoed by subsequent Marxist theoreticians. Many theoreticians on the political left have followed in emphasising the structural or systemic character of "imperialism". Such writers have expanded the temporal period associated with the term, so that it now designates neither a policy, nor a short space of decades in the late 19th century, but a world system extending over a period of centuries, often tracing its origins to Christopher Columbus and, in some accounts, to the Crusades. As the application of the term has expanded, its meaning has shifted along five distinct but often concurrent axes: the moral, the economic, the systemic, the cultural, and the temporal. These changes reflect-among other shifts in sensibility-a growing unease, even squeamishness, with the fact of power, and specifically, of Western power.

Context: Philosophers in antiquity employed the concept of force in the study of stationary and moving objects and of simple machines, though thinkers such as Aristotle and Archimedes retained fundamental errors in their understanding of force. This was due in part to an incomplete comprehension of the sometimes non-obvious force of friction, and consequently to an inadequate view of the nature of natural motion. A fundamental error was the belief that a force is required to maintain motion, even at a constant velocity. Most of the previous misunderstandings concerning motion and force were eventually corrected by Galileo Galilei and Sir Isaac Newton. With his mathematical insight, Sir Isaac Newton formulated laws of motion that were not improved upon for nearly three hundred years. By the early 20th century, Einstein developed a theory of relativity that correctly predicted the action of forces on objects with increasing momenta near the speed of light, and also provided insight into the forces produced by gravitation and inertia.

Context: Aristotle provided a philosophical discussion of the concept of a force as an integral part of Aristotelian cosmology. In Aristotle's view, the terrestrial sphere contained four elements that come to rest at different "natural places" therein. Aristotle believed that motionless objects on Earth, those composed mostly of the elements earth and water, to be in their natural place on the ground and that they will stay that way if left alone. He distinguished between the innate tendency of objects to find their "natural place" (e.g., for heavy bodies to fall), which led to "natural motion", and unnatural or forced motion, which required continued application of a force. This theory, based on the everyday experience of how objects move, such as the constant application of a force needed to keep a cart moving, had conceptual trouble accounting for the behavior of projectiles, such as the flight of arrows. The place where the archer moves the projectile was at the start of the flight, and while the projectile sailed through the air, no discernible efficient cause acts on it. Aristotle was aware of this problem and proposed that the air displaced through the projectile's path carries the projectile to its target. This explanation demands a continuum like air for change of place in general.

Context: Newton's First Law of Motion declares that objects continue in motion at a constant velocity unless acted upon by an external net force or resultant force. This law is an extension of Galileo's insight that constant velocity was associated with a lack of net force (as described in greater detail below). Newton proposed that every object with mass possesses an innate inertia, which functions as the fundamental equilibrium "natural state" in place of the Aristotelian idea of the "natural state of rest". That is, the first law contradicts the intuitive Aristotelian belief that a net force is required to keep an object moving with constant velocity. By making rest physically indistinguishable from non-zero constant velocity, Newton's First Law directly connects inertia with the concept of relative velocities; specifically, in systems where objects are moving with different velocities, it is impossible to determine which object is "in motion" and which object is "at rest". In other words, to phrase matters more technically, the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame of reference, that is, in all frames related by a Galilean transformation.

Context: For instance, while traveling in a moving vehicle at a constant velocity, the laws of physics do not differ from those when at rest. A person may throw a ball straight upward and catch it again as it falls, without the need to apply any force in the direction of the vehicle's motion. This remains true even though another person who observes the moving vehicle pass by perceives the ball to trace a curving parabolic path in the same direction as that of the vehicle's motion. It is the Inertia of the ball, associated with its constant velocity in the direction of the vehicle's motion, which ensures that the ball continues to move forward even as it is thrown upward and falls back down. From the standpoint of the person in the car, the vehicle and everything within it is at rest; it is the outside world that moves with a constant speed in the opposite direction. Since no experiment can distinguish whether it is the vehicle that is at rest or the outside world that is at rest, the two situations are regarded as physically indistinguishable. Inertia thus applies equally to motion at constant velocity as it does to rest.

The two persons might be pulling against one another, as in a tug of war, or they might be pulling in the same direction. In this simple one-dimensional case, without knowledge of the direction of the forces, it is impossible to determine whether the net force results from adding the two magnitudes together or from subtracting one from the other. The association of forces with vectors serves to avoid such difficulties.

The magnitude of this resultant varies from the difference to the sum of the magnitudes of the two forces, in accordance with the angle between their lines of action. Nevertheless, should the forces act upon an extended body, their lines of application must also be specified so as to account for their effects upon the body's motion.

Context: Forces, in addition to being combined, may likewise be resolved into independent components situated at right angles to one another. It follows that a horizontal force directed towards the northeast can be divided into two separate forces, one pointing north and the other east. The summation of these component forces by means of vector addition produces the original force. To resolve force vectors into components relative to a set of basis vectors is frequently a more mathematically elegant method of describing forces than to employ magnitudes and directions. This arises because, in the case of orthogonal components, the components of the vector sum are uniquely determined by the scalar addition of the components of the individual vectors. Orthogonal components are independent one of another, inasmuch as forces acting at right angles to each other exert no influence upon the magnitude or direction of the other. The selection of a set of orthogonal basis vectors is often undertaken with a view to which set will render the mathematics most convenient. It is desirable to choose a basis vector that lies in the same direction as one of the forces, for that force would then possess only a single non-zero component. Orthogonal force vectors may be three-dimensional, with the third component situated at right angles to the other two.

Context: Dynamic equilibrium was first described by Galileo, who observed that certain assumptions of Aristotelian physics were contradicted by observation and reason. Galileo realised that simple velocity addition implied that the notion of an "absolute rest frame" had no existence. Galileo concluded that motion at a constant velocity was wholly equivalent to rest. This stood in opposition to Aristotle's concept of a "natural state" of rest, towards which objects of mass naturally inclined. Simple experiments demonstrated that Galileo's apprehension of the equivalence between constant velocity and rest was correct. For example, were a mariner to drop a cannonball from the crow's nest of a ship proceeding at a constant velocity, Aristotelian physics would have the cannonball fall straight down whilst the ship moved beneath it. Thus, in an Aristotelian universe, the falling cannonball would alight behind the foot of the mast of a ship in motion. However, when this experiment is in fact performed, the cannonball invariably falls at the foot of the mast, as though it were cognisant of the need to accompany the ship notwithstanding its separation. Since no forward horizontal force is applied to the cannonball during its descent, the sole conclusion remaining is that it continues to move with the same velocity as the vessel throughout its fall. Thus, no force is necessary to maintain the cannonball in motion at the constant forward velocity.

Context: The formulation of fundamental theories regarding forces advanced through the unification of disparate ideas. For instance, Isaac Newton, in his universal theory of gravitation, unified the force that causes objects to fall at the Earth's surface with that which governs the orbits of celestial bodies. Michael Faraday and James Clerk Maxwell demonstrated that electric and magnetic forces are unified within a single consistent theory of electromagnetism. During the 20th century, the development of quantum mechanics resulted in the understanding that the first three fundamental forces-all save gravity-constitute manifestations of matter (fermions) interacting through the exchange of virtual particles known as gauge bosons. The standard model of particle physics supposes a likeness among these forces and directed scientists to foresee the unification of the weak and electromagnetic forces in electroweak theory, which was subsequently verified by observation. The full formulation of the standard model anticipates a Higgs mechanism that has not yet been observed; nonetheless, observations such as neutrino oscillations reveal that the standard model remains incomplete. A Grand Unified Theory, which would permit the combination of the electroweak interaction with the strong force, is regarded as a possibility, with candidate theories such as supersymmetry put forward to address some of the unresolved problems in physics. Physicists continue to endeavor to formulate self-consistent unification models that would unite all four fundamental interactions into a comprehensive theory of everything. Einstein endeavored and failed in this undertaking, yet at present, the most widely accepted approach to resolving this matter is string theory.:212-219

Context: It has long been accepted that general relativity constitutes the theory most satisfactorily explaining gravity. In this theory, gravity is not regarded as a force; instead, objects moving freely in gravitational fields proceed under their own inertia in straight lines through curved space-time, which is defined as the shortest space-time path between two events. From the viewpoint of the object, all motion occurs as though no gravitational influence were present. It is only when the motion is observed in a global sense that the curvature of space-time can be perceived, and the force inferred from the object's curved path. Thus, the straight-line path in space-time is seen as a curved line in space, and is termed the ballistic trajectory of the object. As an example, a basketball thrown from the earth moves in a parabola, since it is in a uniform gravitational field. Its space-time trajectory (when the additional ct dimension is included) is almost a straight line, slightly curved, with a radius of curvature of the order of a few light-years. The time derivative of the changing momentum of the object is what is designated as the "gravitational force".
